title: Some Volcanic Clays Kill Bacteria
main_content:
American researchers have discovered how different clays work as medicine. They are researching the effectiveness of clays against antibiotic-resistant infections.

Lynda Williams is a clay and mineral scientist. She works at Arizona State University’s School of Earth and Space Exploration in Tempe. She and her research team have been studying the Aboriginal people of Australia.

“There is evidence of Aboriginals using clays for treating wounds. Many cultures eat clays to settle their stomach.”

Williams and her team found the clay was effective against some pathogens. Pathogens are bacteria and viruses that cause disease. They examined bacteria that have developed resistance to other antibiotics.

In laboratory tests, they saw how a blue-colored clay is effective against the drug-resistant Staphylococcus aureus, known as MRSA. MRSA is a dangerous and sometimes deadly skin infection.

The clay was also effective in treating Buruli ulcer, a skin disease.

Williams says she hopes the study will interest drug companies.

options: A clay and mineral scientist at Arizona State University
A graduate student of Aboriginal studies

options: To obtain minerals for strong bones
As a traditional ritual for healing
